5-meo-dmt.note: Both quotes are on the page under 'What are psychedelic substances?', and the line says no more than they do. For someone who has only heard the name, this first line does not yet say what the drug is: it leans on the family word 'psychedelics' without saying what it means. The same section gives words that could carry that (the effect of classical psychedelics is "often referred to as an ‘altered state of consciousness’"), but that passage is not among this line's anchors, so I have not added it; it would need its own anchor and check.

Quote confirmed (it is the bracket of the 5-MeO-DMT list item). The line stays close to the page's bracket phrase, but apart from the two names only three ordinary words in a row are shared ('a component of'), so I leave it. The page does not say what Bufo alvarius is (it never says 'toad') or what yoppo is, so the line cannot explain them from this anchor: a newcomer will not learn much from it as it stands. If the editor wants a plainer verb, 'It is found in the venom of Bufo alvarius and in ‘yoppo’.' says the same.

5-meo-dmt.line: Counted together with DMT, it is among the psychedelics most often tested in trials for mental health conditions.
5-meo-dmt.note: Both quotes confirmed; they are two parts of one sentence that begins 'To date, the most commonly trialled psychedelics for mental health conditions have been'. The page names one entry, 'DMT (including 5-MeO-DMT)'. 'With DMT, it is among…' can be read as saying 5-MeO-DMT by itself is among the most trialled, which is a little more than the page says; the fix keeps the grouping explicit and replaces 'trialled' with plainer words. Not a risk or how-to line; it is the nearest the page comes to 'is it a medicine'.

amphetamine.line: Amphetamine is a lab-made stimulant: a drug that makes the brain more active.
amphetamine.note: All four quotes are on their pages under the stated headings (FRANK's is the opening text under the page heading 'Amphetamine'). The line's second half is ADF's stock sentence, twelve words in a row ('they speed up the messages travelling between the brain and the body'), so it is not in our own words. The fix says what 'stimulant' means in short words of our own, from EUDA ('a stimulant of the central nervous system') and in keeping with ADF. I made it singular: 'lab-made' rests only on EUDA's 'A synthetic substance', which is said of amphetamine itself, and ADF's section does not say how amphetamines are made. FRANK's 'keeps people alert' is left to the next line, which already says alert.

ADF's two items stand in the list after 'Effects can include:' under 'Effects'; FRANK's lead-in is followed by the items alert, energised, wide awake, excited. The line says no more than these and keeps their hedge.

ADF's sentence goes on 'and narcolepsy' after the second quote. EUDA's sentence ends '(ADHD)' just after the quoted words. The line follows the order of ADF's sentence but is reworded (five of its words in a row at most, around the name dexamphetamine), so I leave it.

amphetamine.line: Amphetamines come as powder, paste, crystals, capsules or tablets; on the street, amphetamine sulphate is called speed.
amphetamine.note: All five quotes confirmed (FRANK prints a curly apostrophe in 'It’s'). The second half of the line is FRANK's sentence word for word, eight words in a row ('Speed is the street name for amphetamine sulphate'); the fix says the same in our own words. 'They' is replaced by 'Amphetamines' so the line does not seem to speak of the medicines in the line before it.

ketamine.note: All four quotes are on their pages under the stated headings. ADF's second sentence ends 'from their body or physical environment', which is what 'dissociative' means; the line leaves that to the next line. A newcomer learns what ketamine is from this line (an anaesthetic that doctors and vets use). 'Ketamine is a dissociative drug' is five words in a row from ADF, the plain way to say it; left.

ADF's two items stand in the list after 'The following effects may be experienced:'; FRANK's item is the first in the list after 'Taking ketamine can make you feel:'; NIDA's sentence begins 'A person using it'. The line says no more than these and keeps their hedge.

ketamine.line: Outside medicine it is usually a white or off-white powder, also called K, ket or special K.
ketamine.note: All five quotes confirmed. ADF's sentence begins 'When it’s sold illegally,' and NIDA's quote follows 'sold as a liquid or off-white powder, and'. The facts are right, but the first half of the line is ADF's sentence with only its opening changed: eight of its words in a row ('usually comes as a white or off-white powder'). The fix changes the verb; the colour and form have to stay as the pages give them. FRANK describes street ketamine as white or brown and grainy, which the line does not use.

anchors.where: Ketamine and mental health (sub-heading; the main heading above it on the page is 'Overdose', not 'Effects of ketamine')
Ketamine and mental health (sub-heading; the main heading above it on the page is 'Overdose', not 'Effects of ketamine')

ketamine.note: The three quotes are exact (ADF's sentence begins 'Currently'). Only the heading path of the two ADF anchors is corrected: the sub-heading 'Ketamine and mental health' is right, but it does not stand under 'Effects of ketamine'. In the page's heading order the main heading 'Overdose' comes between them, followed by the sub-headings 'Coming down', 'Long-term effects', 'Ketamine bladder syndrome' and then this one. The line puts 'treatment-resistant depression' in plain words and says no more than the two pages; it leaves out the nasal spray, which is right for an identity line.

kratom.line: Kratom is a tree from Southeast Asia; products made from its leaves can have stimulant-like and opioid-like effects.
kratom.note: All five quotes confirmed (NIDA prints Mitragyna speciosa in italics; its Highlights sentence begins '“Kratom” commonly refers to'; EUDA's second quote follows 'is a 4 to 16 metre high'). The line says no more than the pages and a newcomer learns what kratom is. A small fix only: 'a tree native to Southeast Asia' is six words in a row from NIDA, right at the limit, so 'native to' becomes 'from'. The rest is reworded enough.

The two quotes are consecutive parts of one sentence that begins 'Researchers have found that'. That sentence goes on to stopping or reducing other drug use; the line rightly leaves that out. Hedge kept ('people report').

kratom.line: It comes as dried leaves, crushed or ground to powder, and as capsules, extracts or tea.
kratom.note: All four quotes confirmed (EUDA's third begins 'Traditionally,'). NIDA's sentence is about how people take kratom; the line uses it only for the forms (tea, extract), which is right. A small fix only: 'as crushed or powdered dried leaves' is six words in a row from EUDA's 'Physical form', right at the limit; the fix says the same in another order. The pages say the leaves are made or brewed into tea, so 'comes as tea' is a loose but fair way to put it.

EUDA's clause begins 'There is, however,'; NIDA's Highlights bullet begins 'While'. The line says no more than these. It keeps EUDA's 'no approved use … in modern medicine' with the middle left out (three words, then three), which is under the limit, so I leave it; if the editor wants more distance, 'It is not approved as a medicine.' says the same.

methylphenidate.note: All five quotes confirmed on NHS (above the first sub-heading), MedlinePlus ('Why is this medication prescribed?') and NIDA (entry 'Methylphenidate'). The line says no more than they do, in our own words, and a newcomer learns what methylphenidate is.

methylphenidate.line: It makes the brain more active, mostly in the parts that help with attention and behaviour.
methylphenidate.note: Quote confirmed; the NHS sentence begins 'They work by' (said of stimulants as a group, to which the page says methylphenidate belongs). The line is that sentence with a few words changed: 'works by … activity in … the brain', then six words in a row ('that help control attention and behaviour'). The fix says the same and keeps the page's 'particularly' as 'mostly'.

NIDA's sentence begins 'People may misuse methylphenidate' and ends at 'appetite' (the page prints curly quotation marks around high); it carries all three reasons, and the line puts 'misuse' in neutral words. ADF's sentence begins 'New research has explored the potential side effects of using Ritalin®': it speaks of the brand, and the page never says that Ritalin is methylphenidate, though the same section lists methylphenidate first among 'ADHD medications used as nootropics'. So ADF supports only the school part, and loosely.

NHS and MedlinePlus carry the whole line: NHS says 'It comes as standard tablets' just before the first quote and prints the brand names inside its main heading; MedlinePlus lists the forms, and its 'Brand names' list has Concerta® and Ritalin® (Ritalin marked as discontinued there). The ADF anchor does not support the line: the quoted words are on the page under 'ADHD medications', but that 'Brand names' line covers three ADHD medicines together (it goes on 'Ritalin 10®, Dexamphetamine tablets®, Vyvanse®') and the page nowhere says which brand is methylphenidate. It should not be shown as a source for this line. Here I differ from the first reader's notes, which count this page for two anchors: it serves for the line before this one, not for the brand names.

prescription-opioids.line: Opioids act on the body's opioid receptors, including in the brain; some come from the opium poppy, others are lab-made.
prescription-opioids.note: All three quotes confirmed. ADF's two are parts of one sentence, joined by 'and any'; NIDA's goes on 'the spinal cord, and throughout the body'. The facts are right, but the first half of the line is ADF's defining clause: eight of its words in a row ('on opioid receptors in the brain and body'). The fix says the same in another order. For a newcomer this first line does not say what prescription opioids are: it defines the family through 'opioid receptors', which it cannot explain. The next line ('medicines used mainly to treat pain') does that job and would serve better as the first line.

NIDA's sentence is exact under the entry 'Opioids'. FRANK's first quote follows 'Opioid painkillers are'; its second follows 'They might be prescribed for moderate or severe pain'. ADF's sentence stands under the bold label 'Opioid pain medications' and follows 'these medications are prescribed to treat different types of pain'. The line says no more than these; it is close to NIDA's short sentence but reworded, with no six-word run.

FRANK's 'Also called' line is exactly as quoted. ADF's lead-in is followed by the list Buprenorphine, Codeine, Fentanyl, Methadone, Morphine, Oxycodone, Tramadol (most with brand names in brackets). ADF's forms sentence begins 'Pharmaceutical (medical) opioids' and goes on with tablets or capsules, liquids, syrups and injectable solutions. The four names and five forms are all on the pages; the forms are listed as forms of medicines, with no how-to.

FRANK's sentence is exact under 'How does it make you feel?'; ADF's two items stand in the list after 'The immediate effects of opioids can include:'. The line says no more than these and keeps the hedge. 'Relaxed, calm and sleepy' is four words in a row from FRANK, under the limit. ADF's list is about opioids as a class (medicines and others); FRANK's sentence is about opioid painkillers themselves.

psilocybin.note: All seven quotes confirmed under the stated headings (FRANK's also appears a second time under 'What does it look like?'; EUDA's names follow 'Common names in the English language are:'). The line says no more than the pages, in our own words, and a newcomer learns what psilocybin is; the next line says what 'psychedelic' means in practice.

psilocybin.line: It can change mood, thoughts and the senses: people can see colours, hear sounds and experience time very differently.
psilocybin.note: All three quotes confirmed (ADF's sentence carries a footnote mark after the full stop). The facts are right and hedged. But the second half of the line is FRANK's sentence with three words taken out: all eight of its words ('colours, sounds and time can seem very different') come from that sentence in the same order. The fix says the same in our own words.

All five quotes confirmed. ADF's powder sentence goes on 'that can be processed into tablets or capsules or dissolved in water', which the line rightly leaves out. EUDA's sentence runs 'deliberately dried, cooked, frozen)' between the two quoted parts. The line says no more than the pages.

All three quotes confirmed. In ADF's sentence 'This' points back to 'Psilocybin may increase the brain's ability to create new emotional and information pathways'. The line keeps NIDA's hedges ('evidence', 'may') and says no more. It follows the shape of NIDA's two sentences with other words (studying for investigating, possible for potential, help with for be an effective treatment for); no six-word run, so I leave it.

salvia-divinorum.note: All six quotes confirmed under the stated headings (ADF's first follows 'Salvia (salvia divinorum)'; EUDA's first follows 'The psychoactive plant Salvia divinorum, or the ‘diviner’s sage’,'; FRANK's opening sentence goes on 'that produce hallucinations when chewed or smoked', which the line rightly leaves out). The line says no more than the pages, in our own words, and a newcomer learns what salvia is.

salvia-divinorum.line: It can bring on a short but strong psychedelic experience, with hallucinations.
salvia-divinorum.note: All four quotes confirmed (ADF's list item stands after 'Effects may include:' under 'Effects of salvia' > 'Effects'). The facts are right and hedged, but the main clause is ADF's phrase word for word, six words in a row ('can cause brief, intense psychedelic experiences'). The fix says the same in our own words.

salvia-divinorum.line: Indigenous shamans in Mexico have long used it; it has no approved use as a medicine.
salvia-divinorum.note: All three quotes confirmed (EUDA's first follows 'where the Mazatec Indians ingest its fresh leaves or leaf preparations'). The facts are right, but the first half of the line is ADF's clause word for word, eleven words in a row ('has a long history of use by Indigenous shamans in Mexico'). The fix says the same in another order; the second half is unchanged. 'No approved use' rests on EUDA alone, in a profile dated 2012, as the first reader also says: the editor may want a newer page before stating it in the present tense.

All five quotes confirmed (EUDA prints curly apostrophes and its list follows 'Common names in English are:'; FRANK's sentence also appears a second time under 'How do people take it?'). Forms and names only, no how-to; the line says no more than the pages.

synthetic-cannabinoids.note: All three quotes confirmed. FRANK's is the first sentence under the page heading; NIDA's follows 'Synthetic cannabinoids are a' (the body of that entry lies in the second part of the long A to Z page, which I read from character 100000); ADF's follows 'Cannabinoids include'. The line joins FRANK and NIDA in our own order, with no six-word run, and says no more than they do. A newcomer gets the gist (lab-made, like the chemicals in cannabis); 'cannabinoid receptors' is the one hard term.

synthetic-cannabinoids.line: Researchers first made them in the 1980s while looking for medicines; some are prescribed in some countries.
synthetic-cannabinoids.note: All three quotes confirmed. ADF's first follows 'Synthetic cannabinoids were' and goes on 'with similar therapeutic effects (e.g. nausea and pain relief) to cannabis (THC) and CBD (cannabidiol)'; its third follows 'None of these products are approved for use in Australia,'. The facts are right, but the first half of the line is ADF's clause with only 'who were' taken out: eight words in a row ('were first developed in the 1980s by researchers'), then four more. The fix says the same in our own words; the second half is unchanged.

synthetic-cannabinoids.line: People can feel happy, relaxed, giggly or hungry.
synthetic-cannabinoids.note: All three quotes confirmed (ADF's item stands after 'The effects of synthetic cannabinoids can include:'; FRANK's sentence ends 'and become very talkative'; NIDA's item stands after 'They may include:' under 'How do synthetic cannabinoids make people feel?'). The facts are right and hedged, but the line is FRANK's sentence with small changes: 'feel happy and relaxed' and 'may get the giggles' are both its words, in its order. The fix says the same in our own words.

All six quotes confirmed. ADF's first follows 'Synthetic cannabinoids are'; FRANK's last follows 'Synthetic and semi-synthetic cannabinoids are'; NIDA's follows 'usually added to liquid cartridges used in vaping devices or' and ends 'so they can be smoked', which the line rightly leaves out. The line says how the products come and are named, in our own words, and no more than the pages say.

synthetic-cathinones.note: All six quotes confirmed. FRANK's two are one sentence, the second following the first directly; ADF's first follows 'Synthetic cathinones is the name of' and its second ends 'and the body and have similar effects to amphetamines'; NIDA's follows 'Synthetic cathinones, also known as bath salts, are' (that entry lies in the second part of the long A to Z page, read from character 100000); EUDA's goes on 'one of the psychoactive principals in khat'. The line joins NIDA and FRANK in our own order (five words in a row at most, 'found in the khat plant'), does not repeat ADF's stock sentence, and a newcomer learns what these drugs are.

All three quotes confirmed. ADF's item stands in the list after 'Generally speaking, in small doses the following effects may be experienced' (the line rightly says nothing of doses). The line says no more than the pages and keeps their hedge. It is close to FRANK: every feeling word is FRANK's, in FRANK's order, drawn from two sentences (longest run four words, 'more awake and alert'), which is under the limit, so I leave it. If the editor wants more distance, a line that also uses ADF's words says the same: 'People can feel happy, excited and energetic, more awake and alert, and keen to talk.'

All four quotes confirmed (ADF's first follows 'Synthetic cathinones are mostly'; FRANK's follows 'Most synthetic cathinones are'; EUDA's follows 'Synthetic cathinones are' and ends the sentence). The line says no more than the pages; 'white or brown powders' is four words in a row from ADF, under the limit. FRANK gives the colours as white, off-white or yellowish, which the line does not use.

anchors.where: Explore stimulants on the Drug Wheel > AKA (list: Bath salts, Bubbles, Drone, Flakka, Kitty cat, M-cat, Meow, Meow-meow, Meph, Plant food)

synthetic-cathinones.note: All six quotes are on their pages. Only the place of the ADF one is corrected: 'Bath salts' is the first item of the 'AKA' list in the block 'Explore stimulants on the Drug Wheel' near the end of the page, not under 'What are synthetic cathinones?' (that section's list is of types of cathinones, and 'Bath salts' is not in it). EUDA's names are given for mephedrone, which fits the line. 'Mephedrone is the best-known type' is the first five words of FRANK's sentence, under the limit; left. Names only, no how-to.
